awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Sensing Device for Motion Capture
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this I-Corps project is the development of a motion capture technology to be used in filmmaking and animation. Currently, capturing intricate motions of finger joints has remained a significant challenge. Traditional motion capture technologies, such as optical tracking systems, primarily rely on cameras and reflective markers to track movements. This technology presents several drawbacks as it relies on controlled environments, such as specific lighting conditions, and inaccurate capturing of complex and rapid movements. The new technology addresses these issues by incorporating a wearable, self-powered sensor to capture motion. This application may improve the design of immersive experiences using Extended Reality (XR) technologies. The sensor also may have application in the field of rehabilitation, capturing real-time biomechanical motions. 

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a wearable motion capturing device. The aim is to offer users greater flexibility and adaptability in working in dynamic settings and environments, such as capturing the motion of the human hand. The new technology is based on a textile sensor composed of hundreds of miniatured sensors directly in contact with the human hand. This integration allows the motion data to be genuine and comprehensive and, combined with an algorithm for real-time signal processing, the sensor can track the motion of the user with seamless data transfer. In comparison with optical or Inertial Movement Unit (IMU)-based systems, this device does not require a specifically allocated workspace and is self-powered. This flexibility provides the wearers more freedom to carry on the hand movement tasks in any environment.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Our project aims to address one of the most persistent challenges in filmmaking, animation, and extended reality: capturing the full complexity of human motion, including intricate finger and hand movements. Traditional motion capture systems depend heavily on expensive equipment, controlled studio environments, and restrictive setups. These limitations make it difficult for independent creators and smaller studios to access professional-quality motion capture technology.

To tackle this challenges, our team developed a self-powered, textile-based wearable sensor that can be easily slipped on like a glove. Compare to conventional systems that require cameras, markers, or frequent battery charging, our sensor generates its own power from user movement, offering continuous and reliable tracking. This breakthrough makes motion capture more portable, accurate, and accessible, while also reducing setup costs and technical barriers.

Intellectual Merit
The project advanced fundamental knowledge in self-powered sensing and its applications for motion tracking. By exploring triboelectric textile sensors—materials that convert mechanical motion into electrical signals—we demonstrated their potential to capture fine-grained biomechanical data in real time. We built proof-of-concept prototypes, tested their ability to track hand and finger motion, and showed how they could be integrated with software pipelines used by artists and engineers. These contributions expand the understanding of wearable health technology, human–computer interaction, and real-time biomechanical monitoring.

Broader Impacts
Beyond advancing research, our work focused on lowering the entry barriers for creative and art professionals. Through the NSF I-Corps program, we engaged in extensive customer discovery interviews with independent animators, mid-tier motion capture studios, and industry professionals. These conversations highlighted the need for tools that are affordable, flexible, and easy to integrate into diverse workflows. Our technology directly addresses their needs, empowering a wider range of voices in filmmaking, gaming, and immersive media. By making advanced motion capture more accessible, we aim to foster innovation, creativity, and diversity in storytelling.

The project also created educational opportunities for students and early-career technologists. Team members gained hands-on experience in combining engineering, design, and market research, developing skills essential for future careers in both academia and industry. In addition, the research has potential applications beyond entertainment, such as rehabilitation, ergonomics, and human–machine interaction.

Project Outcomes
Over the course of the award, we designed and built a slip-on wearable glove with embedded self-powered sensors. We conducted proof-of-concept demonstrations showing lifelike recording of hand and finger movements. We Interviewed over one hundred industry professionals to validate the need for affordable, adaptable motion capture. Last, we identified commercialization pathways, including direct-to-consumer products and rental models, particularly targeting mid-tier studios.

In summary, our project demonstrated both the technical feasibility and the market potential of a new class of self-powered wearable sensors for motion capture. The work contributes to scientific knowledge in textile-based sensing while also paving the way for broader access to immersive technologies. By lowering costs and simplifying use, our innovation opens new possibilities for artists, engineers, and educators to create richer, more inclusive digital experiences.
